title: Ionic and Covalent Bonds

cards.b: Table salt, water, diamond, iron: each holds together in a different way. Atoms bond because the bonded arrangement has lower energy than separate atoms. Most atoms bond to reach a full outer shell, the octet rule (eight outer electrons; two for hydrogen and helium).

cards.h: Three ways to settle the electron bill
cards.b:
• Ionic: one atom hands electrons to another.
  • Covalent: atoms share electrons.
  • Metallic: atoms pool electrons in a shared sea.

Which one happens depends on electronegativity, the pull each atom has on electrons. A big difference gives ionic, a small one gives covalent.

Sodium has one outer electron, chlorine needs one. Sodium gives it away:

Na → Na+ + e-, and Cl + e- → Cl-

The opposite charges attract strongly: NaCl. Ions pack into a 3D crystal lattice, not separate molecules.

Metals and non-metals typically make ionic compounds (e.g. MgO, CaCl2).

• High melting and boiling points (strong lattice). NaCl melts at about 801 °C.
  • Hard but brittle: shifting a layer lines up like charges, which repel and crack.
  • Do not conduct as solids; conduct when molten or dissolved, because ions can move.
  • Often soluble in water.

G.N. Lewis, 1916, proposed that atoms share electron pairs. Two hydrogens share a pair to form H2. Oxygen shares two pairs with another oxygen: a double bond (O=O). Nitrogen N2 has a triple bond, which is why it is so unreactive.

Water: oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen. Written H-O-H. Non-metals bond covalently with each other.

In H-Cl, chlorine pulls electrons harder, so the bond is polar: slight negative on Cl, slight positive on H. Equal sharing (H2, Cl2) is non-polar.

In metals, outer electrons are free and form a sea of electrons around positive ions. That explains shine, conduction of electricity and heat, and bendability (malleable and ductile).

Covalent compounds like sugar or wax usually have low melting points and do not conduct. Giant covalent solids, like diamond, are the exception: extremely hard with very high melting points.

Magnesium (2 outer electrons) and chlorine (needs 1). Mg gives 2 electrons, so each Cl takes 1: need two Cl. Formula: MgCl2, made of Mg2+ and 2 Cl-. Charges balance: +2 - 2 = 0.

Calcium with oxygen: Ca2+ and O2-: CaO (quicklime). Aluminium Al3+ with oxygen O2-: swap charges to get Al2O3.

Covalent: carbon needs 4, hydrogen 1, so CH4. Nitrogen needs 3: NH3.

• NaCl is not a molecule. It is a lattice, so we call it a formula unit.
  • Ionic and covalent are not strict boxes. Bonds fall on a scale from fully ionic to fully covalent.
  • Covalent does not mean weak. Diamond is covalent and the hardest natural material. Only the forces between separate molecules are weak.

Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861-1944) made mercurous nitrite in 1896, a stable compound that brought him international recognition. He founded Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works in 1901, among India's first modern chemical companies, and wrote A History of Hindu Chemistry. He showed Indian chemistry could be both research and enterprise.

• Ionic: electron transfer, lattice, high melting point, conducts when molten.
  • Covalent: shared pairs; single, double, triple bonds.
  • Metallic: sea of electrons.
  • Electronegativity difference guides the bond type.
